title: Simple Interest
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn principal, rate, time, simple interest, amount, reverse formulas, comparison problems, ratio-based questions and common placement shortcuts.
learningObjectives: Understand the meaning of principal, rate, time, interest and amount.
Calculate simple interest using the standard formula.
Calculate the final amount after adding interest.
Find the principal when interest, rate and time are known.
Convert months and days into years correctly.
Solve problems involving money becoming double, triple or multiple times.
Compare simple interest earned on different investments.
Solve problems involving money invested in two or more parts.
Use shortcuts commonly applied in placement aptitude tests.

sections.heading: 1. Basic Concepts of Simple Interest
content: Simple Interest is the interest calculated only on the original principal throughout the investment or loan period.
The interest remains the same for every equal time period when the principal and rate do not change.
Unlike compound interest, simple interest does not earn interest on previously accumulated interest.
The final amount is obtained by adding the simple interest to the principal.
formulas: Principal (P) = Original amount invested or borrowed
Rate (R) = Interest rate per year
Time (T) = Duration in years
Simple Interest (SI) = Interest earned or paid
Amount (A) = Principal + Simple Interest

examples.question: A person invests $5,000 and earns $600 as interest. Find the final amount.
A loan amount is $8,000 and the borrower repays $9,200. Find the simple interest paid.

sections.heading: 2. Simple Interest Formula
content: Simple Interest depends directly on the principal, annual rate and time.
If any one of these values increases while the others remain fixed, the simple interest also increases.
The rate must normally be expressed as a percentage per annum and time must be expressed in years.
formulas: P = Principal
R = Annual rate of interest in percent
T = Time in years

examples.question: Find the simple interest on $4,000 at 5% per annum for 3 years.
Find the simple interest on $7,500 at 8% per annum for 2 years.
Find the simple interest on $12,000 at 6% per annum for 4 years.

sections.heading: 3. Finding the Amount
content: The amount is the total money received or repaid at the end of the investment or loan period.
It includes both the original principal and the simple interest.
formulas: Amount = Principal + Simple Interest
A = P + SI

examples.question: Find the amount on $6,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years.
Find the amount on $15,000 at 4% per annum for 5 years.

sections.heading: 4. Finding the Principal
content: When simple interest, rate and time are known, rearrange the basic formula to find the original principal.
Always ensure that time is measured in years before applying the formula.

examples.question: The simple interest is $900 at 6% per annum for 3 years. Find the principal.
A sum earns $1,600 as simple interest at 8% per annum in 4 years. Find the principal.

sections.heading: 5. Finding the Rate of Interest
content: The annual rate can be found when principal, simple interest and time are known.
The answer is expressed as a percentage per annum.

examples.question: A principal of $8,000 earns $1,200 in 3 years. Find the annual rate.
A sum of $10,000 earns $2,400 in 4 years. Find the annual rate.

sections.heading: 6. Finding the Time
content: The investment or loan period can be found when principal, simple interest and rate are known.
The result obtained from the formula is normally in years.

examples.question: How long will $5,000 take to earn $1,000 at 5% per annum?
A sum of $12,000 earns $2,880 at 8% per annum. Find the time.

sections.heading: 7. Converting Months and Days into Years
content: Simple interest rates are generally given per annum, so the time must be expressed in years.
Convert months into years by dividing by 12.
Convert days into years using 365 days, unless the question explicitly uses 360 days.
formulas: Time in years = Number of months / 12
Time in years = Number of days / 365

examples.question: Find the simple interest on $6,000 at 8% per annum for 9 months.
Find the simple interest on $7,300 at 10% per annum for 90 days, assuming 365 days in a year.

sections.heading: 8. When the Amount is Given
content: When amount and principal are given, first find the simple interest by subtraction.
After finding the interest, use the appropriate formula to calculate rate, time or principal.
formulas: SI = Amount − Principal
A = P + SI

examples.question: A sum of $10,000 becomes $12,400 in 4 years. Find the simple interest.
A sum of $8,000 becomes $9,600 in 5 years. Find the rate.

sections.heading: 9. Direct Proportionality in Simple Interest
content: Simple interest is directly proportional to principal, rate and time.
If the principal doubles while rate and time remain fixed, simple interest doubles.
If the rate triples while principal and time remain fixed, simple interest triples.
If the time is reduced by half while principal and rate remain fixed, simple interest is reduced by half.
formulas: SI ∝ P when R and T are constant
SI ∝ R when P and T are constant
SI ∝ T when P and R are constant
SI ∝ P × R × T

examples.question: A sum earns $600 at a certain rate and time. What interest will twice the principal earn at the same rate and time?
examples.solution: Since SI is directly proportional to principal, the interest will also double. Required interest = $1,200.

examples.question: A sum earns $900 in 3 years. How much will it earn in 5 years at the same rate?

sections.heading: 10. Money Becoming Double, Triple or Multiple
content: When a sum becomes double, the interest earned is equal to the principal.
When a sum becomes triple, the interest earned is twice the principal.
When a sum becomes four times, the interest earned is three times the principal.
Under simple interest, the increase is linear with time.
formulas: If Amount = 2P, then SI = P and RT = 100
If Amount = 3P, then SI = 2P and RT = 200
If Amount = 4P, then SI = 3P and RT = 300
Time to become n times = 100(n − 1) / R

examples.question: In how many years will a sum double at 10% simple interest?
examples.solution: For doubling, RT = 100. Therefore, T = 100/10 = 10 years.

examples.question: In how many years will a sum triple at 8% simple interest?
examples.solution: For tripling, RT = 200. Therefore, T = 200/8 = 25 years.

examples.question: At what rate will a sum become four times in 20 years?
examples.solution: For four times, RT = 300. Therefore, R = 300/20 = 15% per annum.

sections.heading: 11. Finding a New Amount after a Different Time
content: Under simple interest, the interest earned per year remains constant.
Find the annual interest first and then multiply it by the required number of years.
formulas: Annual interest = Total simple interest / Number of years
New interest = Annual interest × New time
New amount = Principal + New interest

examples.question: A sum of $5,000 amounts to $6,000 in 4 years. Find the amount after 7 years at the same rate.
examples.solution: Interest in 4 years = $1,000. Annual interest = $250. Interest in 7 years = $1,750. Amount = $5,000 + $1,750 = $6,750.

examples.question: A sum amounts to $9,200 in 3 years and the principal is $8,000. Find the amount after 5 years.
examples.solution: Interest in 3 years = $1,200. Annual interest = $400. Interest in 5 years = $2,000. Amount = $8,000 + $2,000 = $10,000.

sections.heading: 12. Difference Between Amounts at Different Times
content: The difference between two amounts under simple interest is the interest earned during the difference in time.
This method is useful when the principal is not directly given.
formulas: Difference in amounts = Annual interest × Difference in time
Annual interest = Difference in amounts / Difference in years

examples.question: A sum amounts to $7,200 in 3 years and $8,000 in 5 years. Find the annual interest.
examples.solution: Difference in amounts = $800. Difference in time = 2 years. Annual interest = 800/2 = $400.

examples.question: A sum amounts to $11,500 in 4 years and $13,000 in 7 years. Find the principal.
examples.solution: Difference of $1,500 is interest for 3 years. Annual interest = $500. Interest for 4 years = $2,000. Principal = $11,500 − $2,000 = $9,500.

sections.heading: 13. Comparing Two Investments
content: When comparing investments, use the product P × R × T.
The investment with the larger product earns more simple interest.
If the principal is the same, compare only rate × time.
formulas: SI1 : SI2 = P1R1T1 : P2R2T2
For the same principal, SI1 : SI2 = R1T1 : R2T2
For the same rate and time, SI1 : SI2 = P1 : P2

examples.question: Compare the interest on $5,000 at 8% for 3 years and $6,000 at 5% for 4 years.
examples.solution: First SI = $1,200. Second SI = $1,200. Therefore, both investments earn equal interest.

examples.question: The same principal is invested at 6% for 4 years and 8% for 3 years. Compare the interests.

sections.heading: 14. Ratio-Based Simple Interest Problems
content: Ratios can be used to compare principals, rates, times or interests.
Cancel common factors before calculating the final ratio.
formulas: SI1 : SI2 = P1R1T1 : P2R2T2
If rates and times are equal, SI ratio = Principal ratio
If principals and times are equal, SI ratio = Rate ratio
If principals and rates are equal, SI ratio = Time ratio

examples.question: Two principals are in the ratio 3:5 and are invested at the same rate for the same time. Find the interest ratio.
examples.solution: Since rate and time are the same, interest ratio = principal ratio = 3:5.

examples.question: Two sums are in the ratio 2:3, their rates are in the ratio 4:5 and their times are in the ratio 3:2. Find the interest ratio.

sections.heading: 15. Difference Between Two Simple Interests
content: When two investments differ in principal, rate or time, calculate the difference using the simple interest formula.
If only one factor changes, the difference can often be calculated directly.
formulas: Difference in SI = Difference in principal × R × T / 100
Difference in SI = P × Difference in rate × T / 100
Difference in SI = P × R × Difference in time / 100

examples.question: Find the difference between the simple interests on $8,000 and $5,000 at 6% for 4 years.
examples.solution: Difference in principal = $3,000. Difference in SI = (3,000 × 6 × 4)/100 = $720.

examples.question: Find the difference between the interest on $10,000 at 8% and 5% for 3 years.
examples.solution: Difference in rate = 3%. Difference in SI = (10,000 × 3 × 3)/100 = $900.

sections.heading: 16. Money Invested in Two Parts
content: A total amount may be divided and invested at different rates.
Represent one part using a variable and the other part as the total minus that variable.
Add the interests earned by both parts and equate the sum to the total interest.
formulas: First part = x
Second part = Total amount − x
Total SI = SI on first part + SI on second part

examples.question: A total of $10,000 is invested partly at 5% and the rest at 8% for one year. The total interest is $650. Find the amount invested at 5%.
examples.solution: Let the amount at 5% be x. Then 0.05x + 0.08(10,000 − x) = 650. So 5x + 800,000 − 8x = 65,000 after multiplying by 100. Therefore, 3x = 15,000 and x = $5,000.

examples.question: A sum of $20,000 is divided between 6% and 10% simple interest. The total annual interest is $1,600. Find the amount invested at 10%.
examples.solution: Let x be invested at 10%. Then 0.10x + 0.06(20,000 − x) = 1,600. This gives 0.04x = 400, so x = $10,000.

sections.heading: 17. Equal Interest from Different Investments
content: Different principals can earn equal interest if their rates and times compensate for the difference.
Equate the two simple interest expressions and cancel the common factor of 100.
formulas: P1R1T1 = P2R2T2

examples.question: At what rate will $6,000 earn the same interest in 4 years as $8,000 earns at 6% in 3 years?
For how many years should $5,000 be invested at 8% to earn the same interest as $8,000 at 5% for 4 years?

sections.heading: 18. Rate Changes during the Investment Period
content: If the interest rate changes during the investment period, divide the duration into separate parts.
Calculate the simple interest for each period separately and then add the results.
formulas: Total SI = SI for first period + SI for second period + ...
Total SI = P(R1T1 + R2T2 + ...)/100

examples.question: Find the interest on $10,000 for 2 years at 5% and the next 3 years at 8%.
examples.solution: First interest = (10,000 × 5 × 2)/100 = $1,000. Second interest = (10,000 × 8 × 3)/100 = $2,400. Total interest = $3,400.

examples.question: A sum of $8,000 is invested for one year at 6% and two years at 9%. Find the final amount.

sections.heading: 19. Change in Rate or Time
content: If principal remains fixed, the change in interest depends on the change in rate or time.
These questions can often be solved without calculating both complete interest amounts.
formulas: Increase in SI due to rate change = P × Increase in rate × T / 100
Increase in SI due to time change = P × R × Increase in time / 100

examples.question: By how much will the interest on $12,000 for 5 years increase if the rate rises from 6% to 8%?
examples.solution: Increase in rate = 2%. Increase in SI = (12,000 × 2 × 5)/100 = $1,200.

examples.question: By how much will the interest on $10,000 at 7% increase if the time rises from 3 years to 5 years?
examples.solution: Increase in time = 2 years. Increase in SI = (10,000 × 7 × 2)/100 = $1,400.

sections.heading: 20. Placement-Test Strategy
content: Identify which of the five quantities—principal, rate, time, interest and amount—are given.
Convert all time values into years before substitution.
Use ratio and proportionality methods when exact principal values are unnecessary.
For double or triple amount questions, use RT shortcuts instead of calculating full interest.
For changing rates, split the duration into stages.
For two-part investment problems, form one linear equation.
Estimate the answer before selecting an option to detect calculation errors.
formulas: SI = PRT/100
A = P + SI
P = 100SI/RT
R = 100SI/PT
T = 100SI/PR

examples.question: A sum doubles in 8 years under simple interest. Find the rate.
examples.solution: For doubling, RT = 100. Therefore, R = 100/8 = 12.5% per annum.

examples.question: A sum earns $1,500 in 5 years. How much interest will it earn in 8 years at the same rate?
examples.solution: SI is directly proportional to time. Required interest = 1,500 × 8/5 = $2,400.

quickShortcuts.title: Amount
quickShortcuts.note: Amount is always Principal plus Simple Interest.

quickShortcuts.title: Find interest from amount
quickShortcuts.note: Subtract the principal from the amount.

quickShortcuts.title: Months to years
quickShortcuts.note: Divide the number of months by 12.

quickShortcuts.title: Days to years
quickShortcuts.note: Divide the number of days by 365 unless another convention is specified.

quickShortcuts.title: At 10% for one year
quickShortcuts.note: The interest is one-tenth of the principal.

quickShortcuts.title: At 5% for one year
quickShortcuts.note: The interest is one-twentieth of the principal.

quickShortcuts.title: Different amounts at different times
quickShortcuts.note: Their difference gives the interest for the difference in time.

quickShortcuts.title: Changing rates
quickShortcuts.note: Calculate the interest for each period separately.

quickShortcuts.title: Two-part investments
quickShortcuts.note: Let one part be x and the other part be Total minus x.

placementQuestionTypes: Finding interest when amount is given
Finding amount after a different time
Difference between amounts at different times
Rate changing during the investment period
commonMistakes: Using the amount instead of the principal in the simple interest formula.
Adding principal and interest when only simple interest is asked.
Giving simple interest when the question asks for the final amount.
Forgetting to convert days into years.
Using the compound interest formula instead of the simple interest formula.
Treating the rate as a decimal and also dividing by 100.
Applying one rate to the entire period when the rate changes.
Assuming that interest is added to the principal every year.
Using RT = 100 for tripling instead of doubling.
Forgetting that tripling means interest equals twice the principal.
Comparing only rates when principals or times are different.
Using inconsistent currency or time units.
Failing to subtract the principal from the amount before finding interest.
